title: Anycast vs GeoDNS decision log and control-plane state model
content:
Context and purpose:

This doc captures the evaluation and live control-plane design for steering user traffic across regions using Anycast and GeoDNS approaches. Goal is an operationally safe, debuggable pipeline that meets latency SLOs, minimizes cost by preferring local capacity, and provides predictable failover for region outages and congestion events.

High-level decision summary (current leaning):
- Primary routing mode: hybrid. Use Anycast for the majority of latency-sensitive egress (global ingress edge) where BGP-based path selection provides the fastest discovery in many ISPs.
- Regional preference for application backends: control-plane enforces regional affinity via edge->regional mapping (cookie/edge header) and GeoDNS for tiered fallback when Anycast-announced region becomes unhealthy or isolated.
- Use GeoDNS as a safety/fallback layer to steer clients away from persistent regional degradations that Anycast alone cannot express (e.g., partial region capacity shortfall).

Key trade-offs considered:
- Anycast pros: fast failover at network layer, single global IP simplifies TLS certs and client configuration, works well for brief outages and route flaps.
- Anycast cons: visibility is limited (BGP decision is out-of-band), can cause asymmetric routing and traffic blackholes if region announces but internal backends are unhealthy. Hard to force a specific region for certain enterprise customers without source-based routing.
- GeoDNS pros: explicit control per client region, TTL-controlled decisioning, easier to express weighted preferences, integrates with rate-limiting per-region.
- GeoDNS cons: DNS caching delays, local resolver affinity (ISP-local caches) can make changes slow to propagate; risk of stale answers during fast incidents.

Control-plane state model (recommended):
- Node/Region states: ACTIVE, DEGRADED, MAINTENANCE, ISOLATED, DRAINING, OFFLINE.
- Global view state machine: Evaluator collects health signals (BGP reachability, backend health, capacity headroom, latency SLOs) -> computes region score -> moves region into one of the above states.
- Transition rules (high level):
  - ACTIVE -> DEGRADED: p95 latency > target OR error rate > threshold for 3m window OR backend CPU > 80% sustained for 5m.
  - DEGRADED -> ISOLATED: external network path anomalies detected (BGP withdraws from >10% of upstreams) OR failed health-probe across edge routers > 2m.
  - ANY -> MAINTENANCE: manual admin action / scheduled.
  - DRAINING triggers traffic shift policy (see below) and prevents new VIP peering announcements.

Routing/steering policies implemented by control-plane:
1) Prefer-local: map client-region -> nearest region with ACTIVE state. If local region is DEGRADED, allow short burst routing to local until p95 crosses emergency threshold.
2) Weighted spillover: when capacity headroom < X% (configurable), spillover traffic with weights computed from region capacity and current latency. Spillover uses Anycast first then GeoDNS TTL reduce if prolonged.
3) Emergency isolation: if state ISOLATED or OFFLINE, withdraw Anycast announcements for that POP and issue GeoDNS removal (zero weight).
4) Canary routing: rollout a new edge variant to a small fraction via weighted GeoDNS + Anycast origin tag, expand after 15m stable.

How Anycast and GeoDNS work together (mechanics):
- Normal: Global Anycast IP owned by Redwood edge fabric announces from all POPs. Edge load balancer uses local endpoint mapping to route to a regional cluster according to local preference mapping header.
- Degraded local cluster: Edge will keep Anycast up for network-level reachability but mark the backend mapping as DEGRADED and implement local rate-limits and a small fraction (e.g., 15%) of traffic diverted to secondary regions instantly via backend mapping decisions.
- Prolonged or ISOLATED: Control-plane withdraws BGP announcement for the POP (so that upstreams stop routing to it). At the same time GeoDNS is updated: the pool attached to that region is removed or weight set to zero. TTL set conservatively low (30s) during incident windows to force resolvers to pick new answers where possible.

DNS TTL policy:
- Normal: 60s for critical endpoints to balance cache load vs agility.
- Post-incident: 30s for 10 minutes after state transition to speed recovery.
- For enterprise customers that require long-lived IPs, provide static VIP mapping + route-server peering options (enterprise private peering).

Health and probing strategy (why different from other notes):
- Multi-probe model: combine active HTTP probe (from public vantage points), internal synthetic traffic (from edge->regional path), and BGP adjacency monitoring. A single probe failure doesn't flip state; use quorum across different probe types.
- Probing cadence: HTTP probe every 20s, internal synthetic every 10s, BGP session checks every 30s.
- Probe-origin diversity: use 6 vantage points per region spread across major clouds and colos to avoid single ISP-induced false positives.

Telemetry surface (ops needs):
- Per-region metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, error-rate (5xx, 4xx), capacity headroom, inbound bandwidth, active connections, BGP-announcement-count, probe-fail-count.
- Alerts: automated alert if region moves to DEGRADED AND remaining capacity < 20% OR if two regions are DEGRADED simultaneously.
- Dashboard: time-series with annotated control-plane state transitions, a live map of BGP announcements, and DNS answer distribution (by resolver ASN).

Control-plane implementation notes (practical):
- Single reconciliation loop service (k8s controller): reads metrics from TSDB, writes desired actions to a message queue which worker processes convert to concrete actions: BGP route operator, DNS API, edge config push.
- Idempotency: actions must be idempotent; use operation tokens in edge-api to prevent flapping.
- Safety throttle: limit to 1 region state downgrade per 30s to avoid cascading churn.
- Audit log: every decision stored with reason code and raw metric snapshot to make postmortems deterministic.

Operational playbook snippets (draft):
- Short outage (<= 2m, single POP): rely on Anycast; monitor for client perception; no DNS change.
- Sustained backend problem (>= 5m) or capacity shortfall: mark DEGRADED, start weighted spillover (immediate internal routing changes, reduce DNS TTL to 30s), communicate incident to oncall.
- Network isolation (BGP withdraws or complete peering loss): withdraw BGP announcement, update DNS to remove region pool, open P0 incident.

Rollout and testing plan:
1) Lab simulation: simulate BGP withdraws and synthetic backend errors; verify control-plane state transitions and that worker actions (BGP withdraw, DNS update) happen in correct order.
2) Internal canary: pick a subset of low-traffic ASNs and run the hybrid model for 48h. Observe resolver behavior and DNS cache propagation.
3) Progressive expansion: add more ASNs and then a small production percentage (1% traffic) with close SLO monitoring.

Open questions / TODOs:
- TTL grind: what is empirical DNS cache TTL behavior from major ISPs for 30s vs 60s answers? Run measurement job.
- Anycast withdraw impact: measure convergence time across major upstreams when we withdraw a POP announcement. Create JIRA for capture (JIRA-PF-989).
- Enterprise static IP path: define onboarding flow and cost model for enterprise VIPs.
- Edge mapping security: how do we cryptographically assert region mapping tags to prevent MITM or accidental misrouting?

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep GeoDNS updates as a last-resort control — prefer network-layer solutions but be pragmatic.
- Ensure operator UI clearly shows "why" control-plane chose to withdraw a POP (BGP vs backend health).
- Add a small backpressure buffer before draining to avoid flapping in noisy signals.

Appendix: short glossary
- Anycast: BGP announcement of same IP from multiple POPs so routing chooses the closest path.
- GeoDNS: DNS-based answers that vary by client location or resolver ASN to steer them to preferred pools.
- POP: Point-of-presence/Edge location.
- DEGRADED vs ISOLATED: DEGRADED means internal problems (latency/cpu/errors); ISOLATED indicates network-level reachability issues.

References and measurement links:

- github.com/redwood-inference/edge-probes (probe harness)
